title: Extensible Prioritization Scheme for HTTP
summary: Describes a scheme for an HTTP client to tell a server how it would like responses prioritized, and for a server to hint to intermediaries how its responses should be prioritized. It defines the Priority header field and HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 frames for reprioritizing, sharing an extensible format. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A browser tells the server which things it wants first, such as the page before the pictures.

questions: what is the priority header field
subtitle: A simple, extensible way for HTTP clients and servers to say which responses matter most.

tldr.problem: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 multiplex many responses on one connection, so something must decide which gets bandwidth first. The older RFC 7540 priority tree was complex, poorly deployed and ill-suited to HTTP/3.
tldr.mechanism: Priorities are two simple absolute parameters, urgency (0 to 7) and incremental (true or false), sent in a Priority header field and updated later with a PRIORITY_UPDATE frame in HTTP/2 or HTTP/3.
tldr.outcome: The signals are only suggestions, so servers may combine them with other information. It is a Proposed Standard and is not obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 9218 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2022, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the alternative to the stream priorities of RFC 7540, which HTTP/2 has deprecated.

sections.title: Why Responses Need Priorities
sections.content:
HTTP resources often depend on other resources. Rendering an HTML document may be blocked by a CSS file it refers to, while inline images do not block rendering and are drawn incrementally as chunks arrive. Because HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 multiplex many requests and responses in one connection, the sender must choose what to send first.

This RFC defines an extensible prioritization scheme that uses absolute values. It has three pieces: priority parameters (Section 4), the Priority header field, which is an end-to-end signal independent of the HTTP version, and version-specific PRIORITY_UPDATE frames for changing the priority after a request is sent.

The RFC is clear that these signals are input to a server's scheduling and are only a suggestion. They do not guarantee any particular processing or transmission order.
sections.plainLanguage: When many things are being delivered through one pipe, someone has to decide the order. This RFC gives the receiver a simple way to say what it needs first.

sections.title: Replacing RFC 7540 Stream Priorities
sections.content:
The previous scheme from RFC 7540 had clients signal stream dependencies and weights that describe an unbalanced tree. The RFC says it suffered from limited deployment and interoperability and has been deprecated in a revision of HTTP/2. It was also expressed relative to other requests on the same connection, which is hard to fit into protocols such as HTTP/3 that lack strong ordering guarantees across streams. It offered servers no way to signal priority to intermediaries, and experiments from independent research showed simpler schemes can reach at least equivalent performance.

To let endpoints opt out, the RFC defines the HTTP/2 setting SETTINGS_NO_RFC7540_PRIORITIES, whose value MUST be 0 or 1 (initial value 0). Endpoints that use it MUST send it in the first SETTINGS frame and MUST NOT change it. A server that receives the value 1 MUST ignore HTTP/2 priority signals.

Until a client has seen the server's SETTINGS, it SHOULD send both kinds of signal. Once it sees the value 1 it SHOULD stop sending the old HTTP/2 signals, and if the setting is 0 or absent it SHOULD stop sending PRIORITY_UPDATE frames, though it MAY keep sending the Priority header field.
sections.plainLanguage: The old system asked for a complicated family tree of what depends on what, and hardly anyone used it well. The new one is just two easy questions about each item.

sections.title: Urgency and Incremental
sections.content:
Priority information is a set of key-value pairs, encoded as a Structured Fields Dictionary (RFC 8941). Unknown parameters, out-of-range values and values of unexpected types MUST be ignored. Two parameters are defined.

Urgency (u) is an integer from 0 to 7 inclusive, where a smaller value means higher precedence. The default is 3. A client fetching a document made of several resources, such as HTML, SHOULD give the main resource the default urgency so the server can refine it. The lowest level, 7, is reserved for background tasks such as software updates and SHOULD NOT be used for responses that affect user interaction.

Incremental (i) is a Boolean saying whether a response gives useful output as chunks arrive. The default is false. Non-incremental responses of equal urgency are best served one by one, in request order. Incremental ones can be served concurrently, which shares bandwidth but makes each take longer to finish.

New parameters can be registered in the "HTTP Priority" registry. They should not change the meaning of u or i in a way that is not backwards compatible, since older implementations will ignore them.
sections.plainLanguage: Urgency is a number from 0 to 7 for how soon you need something, and 0 is the most urgent. Incremental says whether a partly arrived picture is still useful, like a photo that gets sharper as it loads.

sections.title: The Priority Header and PRIORITY_UPDATE Frames
sections.content:
The Priority header field is a Dictionary of priority parameters that can appear in requests and responses. It is an end-to-end signal, which matters because it lets caching intermediaries store its value with the response. An example request for a CSS file carries priority = u=0, and a JPEG request might carry priority = u=5, i.

The PRIORITY_UPDATE frame is a hop-by-hop signal sent by clients on the control stream. It can reprioritize a response or push stream, or signal the initial priority instead of the header field. It carries a complete set of parameters, and omitting one means its default value. Servers MUST NOT send these frames, and a client that receives one treats it as an error.

  • In HTTP/2 the frame type is 0x10 and its Stream Identifier MUST be zero. It carries a 31-bit Prioritized Stream ID and the Priority Field Value.
  • In HTTP/3 the frame types are 0xF0700 for request streams and 0xF0701 for push streams, and it carries a Prioritized Element ID.

A PRIORITY_UPDATE can arrive before its stream opens, so servers SHOULD buffer the most recently received frame and apply it once the stream is open.
sections.plainLanguage: The sticky note on a request is the header. If you change your mind later, you can send a second note, the update, saying that picture is now the most urgent.

sections.title: Reprioritizing and Merging Signals
sections.content:
A client may want to change its mind after sending a request. The RFC gives the example of a browser that prefetches a JavaScript file with u=7 (background) and then, when the user navigates to a page that needs it, sends a reprioritization with u=0.

Servers often know more than clients, for instance which inline image a page depends on, or that a font should come before images of equal urgency. An origin can therefore send its own Priority response header field, and an intermediary can use it together with the client's request header as input. The RFC gives no guidance on how to merge them. One difference matters: omitting a parameter in a response means the server does not want to change the client's value, while omitting it in a request means the default applies.

In the RFC's non-normative example, a client asks for u=5, i and the origin replies u=1. The intermediary might use urgency 1 but still treat the response as incremental, since the server did not override it.

Clients MAY also use the values to schedule the requests they themselves send.
sections.plainLanguage: The server may know something the browser does not, so it can write its own note. If the server only changes one thing on the note, the other things stay the way the browser wrote them.

sections.title: Server Scheduling and Fairness
sections.content:
Server scheduling uses many inputs and priority is only one. It is RECOMMENDED that servers respect urgency, sending higher-urgency responses first, and respect the incremental parameter when possible. Non-incremental responses of the same urgency SHOULD be served in ascending stream ID order, and incremental ones SHOULD share bandwidth. Servers are urged to avoid starvation, such as a large non-incremental response blocking a small incremental one at the same urgency.

Several wider concerns are covered:

  • Intermediaries with several backend connections can stall low-priority requests if they follow priorities strictly, so they can give each request a little bandwidth.
  • Retransmission over QUIC may compete with new data, and the RFC leaves the choice to the transport.
  • Fairness can suffer when an intermediary coalesces requests from several clients into one connection, since one client's signals could delay all responses for another. A server can check for headers such as Forwarded or Via to detect an intermediary.
  • A server may deliberately deprioritize connections that carry only background traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: A good delivery driver brings the most urgent boxes first but also makes sure no customer waits forever. Fair sharing means one pushy customer cannot hog the truck.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The security section is short. It points to the resource cost of buffering PRIORITY_UPDATE frames (Section 7 of the RFC), and to the examples where servers that prioritize in a certain way might be starved of the ability to transmit responses. It also says the security considerations of Structured Fields apply to parsing the parameters.

For IANA, the RFC registers the Priority header field name, the HTTP/2 setting SETTINGS_NO_RFC7540_PRIORITIES with code 0x9, the HTTP/2 PRIORITY_UPDATE frame type 0x10 and the HTTP/3 frame type range 0xF0700 to 0xF0701. It also creates the "Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Priority" registry, seeded with u and i. Single-character keys need Specification Required, and longer keys use Expert Review.
sections.plainLanguage: The main safety rule is not to let anyone make the server remember too many notes. The RFC also adds the new names to the official lists so nobody uses them for something else.
